newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin sacks Russian armed forces chief of staff.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin sacks Russian armed forces chief of staff.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin on Friday sacked armed forces chief of staff General Mikhail Kolesnikov in what appeared to be part of a purge of the defence ministry's old guard.
No reason was given for the dismissal of Kolesnikov, 57, a long-serving career officer who served as caretaker defence minister for a month earlier this year.
But new Defence Minister Igor Rodionov has been putting his own men into top military posts in a bid to consolidate power.
There did not appear to be any link between Kolesnikov's dismissal and that of security chief Alexander Lebed on Thursday.

The presidential press service said Kolesnikov had been replaced by General Viktor Samsonov, currently in charge of coordinating military cooperation between member states of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS).
Interfax news agency said Kolesnikov would be given Samsonov's job but this could not immediately be confirmed.
Samsonov, 56, served as armed forces chief of staff in 1991 and 1992. He has been in the army since 1960.
Kolesnikov, who was also removed from his post of first deputy defence minister, served as caretaker defence minister between mid-June and mid-July before Rodionov took over.
Kolesnikov had no known links with former security chief Alexander Lebed, whom Yeltsin sacked on Thursday. Rodionov backed Yeltsin's move, saying Lebed had been hard to work with.

In early October Yeltsin sacked several senior generals, including commanders of the paratroop and space forces. The ministry said at least three senior generals had been removed, including a first deputy head of the general staff.
Rodionov's main brief is to try to reform the armed forces, something his unpopular predecessor Pavel Grachev failed to do. The armed forces are deep in debt and many oppose the idea of troop cuts.

Lebed, a former paratroop commander, clashed with Rodionov over plans to slash paratoops forces by up to a quarter. The deputy commander of Russia's airborne forces, Vladimir Kazantsev, was sacked on Thursday for opposing Rodionov.

Kolesnikov was a popular professional soldier with a tough stance on NATO's plans to expand eastwards. He served the length and breadth of the former Soviet Union and its then east European satellite states.
He started as a company commander in the Russian Far East in 1959 after graduating from a tank school in Omsk, western Siberia. He did not serve in Afghanistan.
Kolesnikov kept a low profile in the 21-month-old war in Chechnya, which badly damaged the reputation of the army and which has cost over 30,000 lives.
